name: Giant's Anchor

detectability.signature: Concentrated gravitational gradient with no corresponding mass source

proximity: Navigation systems detect increasing gravitational pull beginning at approximately 200,000 km
Course corrections become necessary to avoid being drawn inward
Nearby debris and dust accumulate in a visible accretion disc around the well's center
contact: Gravitational forces reach 8-12g at the well's nominal boundary, overwhelming standard thrusters
Ship structures experience severe tidal stress as gravity gradient steepens
All objects within the well are drawn toward a central point at approximately 0.4 km/s^2 acceleration
prolonged_exposure: Hull fatigue from sustained tidal forces leads to structural failure within days
Crew experience physiological effects of sustained high-gravity exposure
Escape becomes progressively more difficult as fuel is consumed fighting the pull

age: Estimated 200,000-300,000 years based on accretion disc composition analysis
phenomena: A thin accretion disc of captured debris orbits the central point, faintly visible in reflected starlight
The gravitational source occupies a point less than 1 meter across yet exerts force equivalent to a dwarf planet
Objects that reach the central point do not appear to be destroyed but simply stop, accumulating into a growing mass
Faint graviton emissions suggest the well is maintained by an active mechanism rather than passive mass
hazards: The well is invisible and detectable only by gravimetric sensors, creating a trap for vessels with outdated charts
Escape from within the well's boundary requires thrust capacity exceeding most civilian vessel specifications
The accretion disc contains fast-moving debris that poses collision hazards to vessels attempting rescue operations
opportunities: The point-source gravity generator at the center represents technology of extraordinary sophistication
The accretion disc contains materials drawn from across the local region over hundreds of millennia, creating a natural sample archive
Study of the well's graviton emissions could advance understanding of artificial gravity generation by centuries
known_incidents: The cargo hauler Titan's Burden was caught in the well's pull in 3134 while navigating with outdated charts; the crew spent 19 hours at maximum thrust before escaping, burning 94% of their fuel reserves and giving the anomaly its name
A research probe was deliberately lowered to within 500 meters of the central point in 3203, confirming the active graviton emissions before the probe's signal was lost to gravitational redshift
description: Giant's Anchor is an invisible fist of gravity clenched around a point in empty space. There is nothing to see at its center, no star, no collapsed remnant, no visible object of any kind, yet a volume 250,000 kilometers across pulls at everything within reach with the quiet, implacable force of a dwarf planet. The only visual evidence of its presence is a thin disc of accumulated debris orbiting the central point, glinting faintly in distant starlight like a ring of dust around an absent finger.

The well's gravitational gradient is steep and merciless. Ships that cross the boundary without sufficient thrust capacity are drawn inexorably inward, fighting escalating tidal forces that stress hulls and exhaust fuel reserves. At the center, objects simply stop, joining a slowly growing mass of captured material that has accumulated over hundreds of thousands of years. The gravitational source itself is impossibly compact, less than a meter across, and emits graviton signatures consistent with an active mechanism rather than natural mass, suggesting this is a device rather than a phenomenon.

Giant's Anchor takes its name from the cargo hauler Titan's Burden, whose near-fatal encounter with the well became a celebrated survival story across the shipping lanes. The crew's 19-hour burn at maximum thrust, escaping with barely enough fuel to reach port, captured the public imagination and prompted an extensive survey of the surrounding region. The discovery of the well's artificial nature transformed it from a navigational hazard into one of the most significant archaeological finds of the century, evidence of a civilization capable of creating gravitational anchors of planetary strength.

The well remains a persistent navigational hazard, now well-charted and marked with automated warning beacons at its perimeter. Research operations focus on the central point source, though approaching it is extraordinarily difficult and expensive in terms of fuel and equipment. The accretion disc has become a secondary research interest, as it contains material samples drawn from across the local region over the well's long lifetime, forming an unintentional geological archive. The fundamental questions remain: who built this anchor, what was it meant to hold in place, and is the thing it was anchoring still somewhere nearby.
